context:
The Society of Estates: Fig. 2 in Your Book / Fig. 2, NCERT page 4.
1st estate: clergy.
2nd estate: nobility.
3rd estate: three groups, from rich businessmen and lawyers down to landless labourers and servants.
Within the third estate, some were rich and others poor.
alt: Fig. 2 from the NCERT book (page 4): a diagram of the society of estates. The 1st estate (clergy) is at the top, the 2nd estate (nobility) below it, and the 3rd estate at the bottom in three groups: big businessmen, merchants, court officials and lawyers; peasants and artisans; small peasants, landless labour and servants.
description: A diagram of the Society of Estates in pre-revolutionary France, showing three estates stacked from top to bottom: the clergy (1st estate), the nobility (2nd estate), and the third estate. The third estate is enlarged and split into three groups, from big businessmen, merchants, court officials and lawyers at the top, through peasants and artisans, to small peasants, landless labourers and servants at the bottom, so students should notice that the third estate contained both rich and poor people.

context:
The Society of Estates: The Spider and the Fly / Fig. 3, NCERT page 5: an anonymous etching.
The nobleman sits; the peasant brings grain, fruit and money.
'The nobleman is the spider, the peasant the fly.'
Why did the artist draw the noble as a spider and the peasant as a fly?
alt: Fig. 3 from the NCERT book (page 5), The Spider and the Fly, an anonymous etching: a well-dressed nobleman sits at ease while a poor peasant brings him a bag of money and a basket of produce; a spider's web with a fly hangs in the window above.
description: An anonymous 17th-century French etching shows a seated, richly dressed nobleman with a dog, receiving a money bag, a basket of fruit and a sack of grain from a thin, bearded peasant. A spider web with a spider and trapped fly appears at top left, and a fly is drawn near the verses. Students should notice how the verses and the web image frame the noble as a predator who feeds on the labour of the poor peasant.
text: Plus on a de moyens, plus on en veut avoir / Ce pauvre apporte tout, bled, fruit, argent, volaille / Ce gros Atilord assis, prest a tout receuoir / Ne luy veut pas donner la douceur d'vne cuillerée / A tous Seigneurs tous honneurs. / Maigre comme un leurier d'attache. / Il faut plier ou agréer. / a la mouche / que volle / il ne faut / point dans la toile
